1 # TSD: MRT Application Topology (Single vs Per-Integration) 2 3 ## Document Information 4 5 | Field | Value | 6 | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 7 | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | 8 | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro, Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | 9 | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle, Technical Lead | 10 | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | 11 | **Version** | v0.1 (Draft) | 12 | **Status** | Draft | 13 | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | 14 15 --- 16 17 ## Version History 18 19 | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | 20 | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | 21 | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | 22 23 --- 24 25 ## 1. Problem Statement 26 27 ### 1.1 Context 28 29 The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all 30 server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to 31 integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token 32 validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, 33 SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme 34 (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. Integration build-out begins in the 35 coming sprints. 36 37 ### 1.2 Problem 38 39 How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, 40 has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not 41 a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology 42 determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive 43 to change once integration code exists across many systems. 44 45 Compounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's 46 `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not 47 starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and 48 response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and 49 three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. Seven per-origin connection pools 50 were written to address part of this (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported 51 nowhere and attached to no request. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the 52 in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection. 53 54 ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved 55 56 - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed 57 position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever 58 writes the first proxy. 59 - The missing error handling persists and compounds. It was found by chance in one of the only three 60 server-side integration touchpoints that exist today, and nothing in the codebase, review process, 61 or CI prevents the same pattern recurring as the remaining systems are built. 62 - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback 63 that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. 64 - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking 65 divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. 66 67 ### 1.4 Success Criteria 68 69 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how 70 integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 71 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, 72 with any inaccuracies in existing documentation identified and raised for correction (§7). 73 3. The present failure behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than 74 asserted. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 75 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket. 76 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without 77 re-opening the question. 78 79 --- 80 81 ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions 82 83 ### 2.1 Constraints 84 85 | Constraint | Detail | 86 | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 87 | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. *(Source: MRT Overview, opening constraint statement.)* | 88 | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. *(Source: MRT Overview, Bundles.)* | 89 | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. *(Source: MRT Overview, Projects and Organizations.)* Seven environments are in use: the six deployment tiers plus one ad-hoc test environment *(verified in Runtime Admin, 12 Aug 2026)*. | 90 | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** *(Source: MRT Overview, App Server and Rendering constraints.)* | 91 | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. *(Source: `.docs/prd/regional.md`; `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5 Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture.)* | 92 | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts share a **single first-party origin** (AU at the root, the other seven path-prefixed); the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. *(Sources: `architecture.md` §Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope; MRT Overview, Environments constraints.)* | 93 | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual *(Source: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §9 Performance Strategy; summarised in `.docs/architecture.md` > Pre-Build Decisions #3.)* Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | 94 | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | 95 | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | 96 97 ### 2.2 Assumptions 98 99 | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | 100 | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 101 | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and the number of integration modules the single application carries. | 102 | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | 103 104 --- 105 106 ## 3. Options Analysis 107 108 ### 3.1 Options Summary 109 110 | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | 111 | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 112 | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing deploy pipeline (one workflow per tier: dev, test, sit, uat, stg, prod), version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound operation in any integration blocks every other concurrent request on that process (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | 113 | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | 114 115 ### 3.2 Option Detail 116 117 #### Option A: Single MRT application 118 119 One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All 120 integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single 121 Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by 122 construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one 123 hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its 124 weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than 125 infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). 126 127 #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* 128 129 The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as 130 its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and 131 credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses 132 precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised 133 specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. 134 135 It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or 136 budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications 137 created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a 138 general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as 139 an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent 140 directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own 141 B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable 142 Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for 143 backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an 144 externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in 145 Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment 146 defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a 147 storefront. 148 149 MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or 150 domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. 151 Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently 152 count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every 153 cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and 154 the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight 155 storefronts depend on. 156 157 The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and 158 the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. 159 160 --- 161 162 ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale 163 164 ### 4.1 Recommended Option 165 166 **Option A: Single MRT application, with per-integration safeguards in the server-side layer.** 167 168 ### 4.2 Rationale 169 170 Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off 171 between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an 172 integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A 173 is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost 174 because it is the current state. 175 176 The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of 177 the status quo, because the status quo includes gaps that are real and demonstrated: integration 178 modules do not consistently catch their own failures, three route handlers leave work unobserved, and 179 no upstream call carries a timeout short enough to fail before MRT's own execution ceiling does. 180 Option A is therefore recommended **with safeguards**: one bundle, but with each integration confined to its own module, 181 given its own connection pool with an independent connection cap and timeout budget, wrapped in its 182 own error boundary, and with every route registration observing the promise it starts. These are 183 specified in §5. Adopting Option A without them would settle the topology question while leaving the 184 isolation gap open, which is the state this document exists to close. 185 186 ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted 187 188 - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do 189 not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any 190 integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or 191 configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by 192 infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. 193 - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of 194 deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every 195 integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. 196 - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat 197 environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: anyone 198 who needs deploy or variable access for one integration necessarily has it for all of them. The 199 platform provides no way to scope either within a single project. Accepted; revisit if the team 200 composition changes such that per-integration scoping becomes necessary. 201 - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the 202 module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. 203 204 --- 205 206 ## 5. Technical Implementation 207 208 > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is 209 > deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own 210 > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the 211 > gaps in §1.2 undefined. **Every file listed below is Tier 1 in some form**, so the implementing 212 > ticket must secure approval before starting: `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `config/default.js` are 213 > absolute Tier 1 under Hard Rule #4 (§2.1); the four modules under `overrides/app/ssr/` are Tier 1 214 > Runtime & Integration Config, owned by Integration / SI Partner; and `.claude/rules/` is Tier 1 215 > Governance, requiring both squad leads and the Integration lead. 216 217 ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 218 219 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in 220 `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 221 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under 222 `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 223 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its 224 own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is 225 capped independently of every other integration. 226 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a 227 slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution 228 ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 229 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 230 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it 231 at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a 232 dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful 233 degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 234 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the **entire** promise 235 chain it starts, not merely its final call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved 236 floating promise. Three routes do not do this today (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud 237 failure, or an invalid SLAS callback token, currently produces no response at all rather than an 238 error response. 239 240 ### 5.2 Component / API Changes 241 242 | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | 243 | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | 244 | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the three placeholder origins (`sfccPaymentsPool`, `booxiPool`, and `mulesoftPool`, whose env-var fallback is also a placeholder). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | 245 | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` inside `jwksCaching()`, currently a bare global-dispatcher call. | Modified | 246 | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the `fetch` inside `paymentMetadataHandler()`. | Modified | 247 | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on both `fetch` calls inside `sendMarketingCloudEmail()` (token exchange, then email send). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | 248 | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(absolute Tier 1)** | Attach a `.catch()` to the **whole promise chain** in the passwordless-login and reset-password callback routes, not only to `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)`. `validateSlasCallbackToken` throws on an invalid or expired token (`slasTokens.ts:33,51`) and its chain is equally unobserved, so catching the inner call alone leaves the auth path failing silently. Also observe the `jwksCaching(...)` call in the JWKS route. Three route registrations currently leave a promise unobserved. | Modified | 249 | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | 250 | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | 251 | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | 252 253 ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces 254 255 The contract every integration module must satisfy: 256 257 ```ts 258 // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. 259 import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; 260 261 // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. 262 const response = await fetch(url, { 263 method: 'POST', 264 headers: { /* ... */ }, 265 body: JSON.stringify(payload), 266 dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts 267 }); 268 269 // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. 270 type IntegrationResult = 271 | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } 272 | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; 273 274 // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. 275 app.post(path, (req, res) => { 276 void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { 277 // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered 278 }); 279 }); 280 ``` 281 282 Pool boundaries, origins and connection caps are defined in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 and are 283 deliberately not restated here, to avoid two copies drifting apart. Those caps are derived from 284 expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass 285 described in §9.3 of that document. 286 287 **What the pools add.** Node's `fetch` already creates a separate connection pool per upstream origin 288 by default: `undici`'s `Agent` maintains one `Pool` per origin 289 (`node_modules/undici/lib/dispatcher/agent.js`). A slow integration therefore does not starve an 290 unrelated one, and that is not what explicit pools are for. What the default does **not** provide is 291 a bound on how many connections a single origin may open, or a response timeout short enough to fail 292 before MRT's execution ceiling. Explicit pools add exactly those two things: a **bound** per origin, 293 so one integration under load cannot consume unbounded sockets or overwhelm its upstream, and a 294 **timeout** that lets the integration fail cleanly and return an error rather than the platform 295 terminating the whole request. 296 297 ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases 298 299 | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | 300 | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | 301 | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | 302 | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, so the integration returns an explicit error instead of the whole request being terminated by the platform. | Error | 303 | An integration issues a burst of upstream calls | Its own pool caps the concurrent connections, so the burst queues within that integration rather than opening unbounded sockets and pressuring process file descriptors or the upstream itself. | Edge case | 304 | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | 305 | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | 306 | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation, per the constraint in §2.1. | Edge case | 307 | SLAS callback validation (`jose` fetches the JWKS itself, `slasTokens.ts:38`) | Also outside this pattern: `jose` takes no `dispatcher`. It is not unprotected, however: it applies its own 5s `timeoutDuration` and caches keys for 30s to 10 minutes, so it is low-frequency and already bounded. Left as-is; revisit only if its own defaults prove unsuitable. | Edge case | 308 309 ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes 310 311 No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration 312 adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** 313 `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. 314 315 --- 316 317 ## 6. Testing & Validation 318 319 ### 6.1 Test Coverage 320 321 Mapping to §1.4 criterion 3. Three tests exist and pass today 322 (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`). The table below also specifies two further rows that are 323 deliberately not yet written, and says why. 324 325 | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | 326 | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 327 | Unit / Integration | Asymmetric error handling across the real modules: `sendMagicLinkEmail` and `paymentMetadataHandler` run concurrently against the same upstream failure. | Currently: `sendMagicLinkEmail` rejects out of its module uncaught, while `paymentMetadataHandler` catches its own failure and still responds. After §5: both catch at their own boundary and return an explicit outcome. | 328 | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | 329 | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | 330 | Integration | Once §5 is implemented: that each pool's connection cap is actually enforced under load, and that its timeout fires before MRT's execution ceiling. Note this deliberately does **not** test cross-origin isolation, which §5.3 shows already holds by default. | Concurrency against one origin stays at or below its configured cap; a hung upstream fails through the pool's own timeout and returns an error, rather than running out MRT's 20s/16s ceiling. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | 331 | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | 332 333 Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are 334 already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is 335 already gated in CI. 336 337 ### 6.2 Regression Risk 338 339 The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 340 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to 341 existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and 342 Marketing Cloud email, all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would 343 surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The three tests above cover 344 the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap or timeout tuning, which is why the load-test row is 345 listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the 346 route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. One factor usefully 347 bounds the blast radius of both: a `dispatcher` is passed per call site, so only the four SSR `fetch` 348 calls listed in §5.2 change behaviour. Everything else, including all commerce traffic issued through 349 `commerce-sdk-react`, is untouched by definition. 350 351 --- 352 353 ## 7. === AGENTS.md Graceful Degradation ===
## Graceful Degradation

Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break the whole page. Two defaults override any per-system behaviour: **fail closed on consent** (if consent state is unknown, load no third-party scripts), and **never silently substitute a different checkout, payment, or commerce flow** when an integration is down — surface an explicit error instead.

## Performance

Mobile page speed is a top priority. Every change that touches rendering, data fetching, or assets must not regress it.

- **LCP budget is tight (≤ 2s at p75 mobile)** — Defer every third-party script that isn't required for first paint. Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM, Optimizely, Inside Chat, Narvar EDD, reCAPTCHA, etc.) must not block LCP — use `defer`, `async`, or post-hydration injection. If a new third-party integration looks like it might land on the critical path, flag it before merging.
- **Images:** Always use lazy loading and serve correctly sized images. Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
- **Code splitting:** Prefer dynamic `import()` for heavy components not needed on initial render.
- **Data fetching:** Avoid over-fetching — request only the fields you need. Waterfall requests are not acceptable; parallelise where possible.
- **Bundle size:** Do not introduce large dependencies without confirming with the user.
- **Dependencies:** Before implementing any feature that may require a third-party library, check `package.json` for what is already installed. Evaluate whether an existing dependency can satisfy the requirement. If a better third-party option exists, present the recommendation (existing vs. new, with trade-offs) and wait for user approval before installing anything.

## Gotchas

- **Theme runtime errors:** Custom components (e.g. `ListMenu`) must be defined in the theme object or destructuring will throw.
- **Commerce SDK types not importable:** Check `node_modules/commerce-sdk-isomorphic/dist/` for generated definitions, or declare a narrow local `type`.
- **Magento password migration:** Passwords were not migrated from Magento — all existing customers must reset at go-live. Do not assume any saved credentials exist. Account creation and login flows must handle this gracefully (CFD-013).

=== tsd-architecture.md §12 / §12.1 (lines 445-500) ===
## 12. Graceful Degradation

Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page.

| System                   | Failure mode                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Contentful               | Render page without editorial content; never block commerce data on CMS                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Global-e                 | Surface explicit error; do not silently fall back to SFCC for international checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Didomi                   | Fail closed — no consent, no third-party scripts                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Omneo (writes) / Emarsys | Queue and retry silently; never block the user flow                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Omneo (reads)            | **Load-bearing for My Account profile pages** — per DMU-004 only email + Omneo ID are migrated; all other customer profile data is sourced live from Omneo at login. Surface an explicit retry/error UI on profile pages if the round-trip fails; do not render stale or partial profile data. |
| Google Maps              | Degrade to manual address entry; never hard-block checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| AP21 (Retail Rewards)    | On AP21 unavailability at the point of Rewards application, inform the customer and allow an alternative payment method                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Narvar (EDD)             | Suppress widget; do not show an error or block checkout                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment

The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the _spread_ of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features.

#### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner)

- **Web Application Firewalls + rate limiting** is the primary lever for volumetric attacks and credential-stuffing.
- **SFCC Business Manager** provides API-level rate limiting for SFCC endpoints, independent of the storefront edge.

#### SSR layer (inside the PWA)

`overrides/app/ssr.js` makes server-side `fetch` calls directly (token exchange, JWKS, SF Payments metadata). Node's native `fetch` is backed by `undici` internally. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

> **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach.

The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):

| Pool                   | Origin                                                                                                             | Calls                                                                           | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sfcc-scapi`           | `https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`                                                             | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password)             | 5   | 5 s              | 8 s           | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. Isolated so a JWKS fetch is never starved by higher-volume pools.                                                                                                  |
| `sfcc-payments`        | `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` host (a `*.demandware.net` or SCAPI hostname — waiting confirmation from Mani) | Payment method metadata on every checkout page SSR                              | 10  | 5 s              | 8 s           | Called on every checkout page load; moderate frequency. Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections.                                                                                               |
| `mulesoft`             | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL`                                                                                                | Order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, GiveX balance check | 20  | 5 s              | 10 s          | Highest user-facing concurrency (My Account + PDP). GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
| `marketing-cloud-auth` | `https://{subdomain}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                  | Marketing Cloud client-credentials token exchange                               | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | User-triggered, infrequent; token cached at module scope for 15 min. Isolated so an MC outage cannot consume SFCC or MuleSoft connections.                                                                                                           |
| `marketing-cloud-rest` | `https://{subdomain}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com`                                                                  | Magic-link email send (passwordless login, reset password)                      | 5   | 5 s              | 15 s          | Same trigger as above; higher body timeout because email delivery APIs can respond slowly under load.                                                                                                                                                |
| `google-places`        | `https://places.googleapis.com` (Places API — New)                                                                 | Address autocomplete at checkout (CFD-023, CFD-030, CFD-059)                    | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | Non-critical-path; graceful fallback to manual entry. Short timeouts ensure a Places API slowdown releases connections quickly.                                                                                                                      |
| `booxi`                | Booxi base URL (TBD)                                                                                               | Boutique appointment read in My Account (CRM-165–167)                           | 5   | 3 s              | 5 s           | My Account only; non-critical-path within that page.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content).

---

## 13. Testing Strategy

Three layers, no duplicated coverage — the cheapest layer that proves a behaviour wins.

| Layer                 | Tool             | Covers                                               |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit                  | Vitest           | Pure logic, data mapping, transforms, isolated hooks |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` | Single-component user interactions                   |
| E2E                   | Playwright       | Full journeys, multi-region, integration boundaries  |

=== tsd-architecture.md §9 / 9.3 (355-390) ===
## 9. Performance Strategy

LCP at p75 mobile is the binding constraint and the de-facto cap on third-party script weight.

| Metric                    | Target |
| ------------------------- | ------ |
| LCP (mobile p75)          | ≤ 2 s  |
| Lighthouse Performance    | ≥ 0.80 |
| Lighthouse Accessibility  | ≥ 0.90 |
| Lighthouse Best Practices | ≥ 0.90 |

### 9.1 Third-party defer rule

Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM — which loads Meta, GA4, and other GTM-housed tags via Tell No Lies; Narvar EDD widget; Inside Chat) is deferred, async-loaded, or injected post-hydration so it does not block LCP. **Measmerize** (Find My Size / size guide — PDP only) likewise defers behind LCP — the script injects after the product hero image has loaded. **reCAPTCHA** likewise loads only on register/login form interaction, so it never sits on the critical path of any other page (consent treatment per §11.1). **Exception (AAB-004):** Optimizely Web is a PWA-direct head tag (not a GTM tag) and deliberately loads in the page head **before render** to prevent A/B flicker, scoped to the US storefront where Optimizely runs. **Crazy Egg (AAB-005)** loads async and post-Didomi-consent. Both load strictly post-Didomi-consent; keep both snippets minimal.

### 9.2 Other levers

- **Images:** all storefront imagery — product and editorial — is stored in and served from **Contentful** (`images.ctfassets.net`) via the Contentful Images API; SFCC holds no image assets (DMU-010 migration de-scoped; product images CRM-075; all media via the CMS library HPC-003). The PWA generates `srcset` / `sizes` and sets size, quality, and format per breakpoint on the asset URL — **AVIF primary with WebP / JPEG fallbacks**. Lazy-load all non-LCP images; priority-load the primary hero image (PRD-064). Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
- **Video:** sourced by platform, not self-hosted, so codec / adaptive-streaming selection belongs to the upstream player rather than to this layer:
  - **Product videos → Vimeo**, referenced by embed URL stored in product data or the CMS (PRD-067). Load behind a lightweight facade (poster image + click/scroll-to-load) so the Vimeo player JS never lands on the LCP critical path.
  - **Content-managed page videos → Contentful** by default, served from the Contentful asset CDN and referenced within the CMS content entry alongside the page content. Editorial pages may also embed a Vimeo video by URL where preferred (HPC-004) — the product/editorial split above is the expected pattern, not a hard restriction.
  - Across both: `preload="metadata"` by default; autoplay reserved for muted, short-loop hero clips only.
- Dynamic imports for heavy non-initial components.
- Parallel data fetches; no client-side waterfalls. Fetch only required fields.

### 9.3 Where performance is measured

The CI Lighthouse gate (§14.3) catches regressions but runs against the Dev-tier MRT deployment — slower than production hardware, further from the edge, and not representative of the LCP a real shopper experiences. The signed-off LCP and Lighthouse targets in this section are therefore validated against **Stage**, which mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier). Treat CI numbers as regression indicators; treat Stage numbers as the contractual ones.

> **SSR connection pool tuning:** the initial per-pool connection caps defined in §12.1 are derived from expected concurrency, not observed traffic. The first Stage performance run should include per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics (undici emits these as diagnostic channel events). Use those numbers to validate or revise the caps.

---

## 10. Accessibility

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, with WCAG 2.1 AA as the floor that is always met.

| 1   | Browser & device matrix      | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |

### #1 — Browser & device matrix ✅

**Mobile perf-test floor:** current OS version −2 on iPhone and Android (iOS 17+, Android 14+), verified via BrowserStack Automate. `package.json` browserslist aligned to match.
**Desktop matrix** ([.browserstack.yml](../../.browserstack.yml)): Chrome + Safari (macOS Sonoma), Firefox + Edge (Windows 11) — all latest.

### #2 — Accessibility 🟡

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, at least 2.1 AA. **Automated:** axe-core in Vitest + Playwright; Storybook a11y addon; Lighthouse CI a11y ≥0.90 ([lighthouserc.js](../../lighthouserc.js)). **Manual:** client's existing a11y vendor.
**Pending:** vendor name, screen-reader/browser matrix, audit cadence, remediation owner.

### #3 — Performance budgets ✅

**Client-mandated:** **LCP ≤ 2s** at p75 mobile, plus Lighthouse Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90. These are the only performance numbers in the signed TSD (§9).
**Other CWV (internal working defaults, not client-mandated):** INP ≤ 200ms · CLS ≤ 0.1. Lighthouse mobile defaults at p75.
**CI gate (SIT gate):** Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) asserts the Lighthouse score floors above, plus a >5pt trend-drop gate (LHCI server required). SEO intentionally not asserted. Runs on every PR to `develop` ([`digital-sit.yml`](../../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)), deploys to the **Dev** tier on merge — treat its numbers as a **regression indicator**, not the contractual measurement.
**Contractual measurement:** Client-mandated LCP and Lighthouse numbers are validated on **Stage** — the prod-mimicking tier (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier as production). The Dev tier is slower and further from the edge, so its absolute numbers will be worse — that is expected and not a sign-off concern. Full environment topology in [tsd-architecture.md §14.1](./temp/tsd-architecture.md).
**Bundle ceilings — internal CI policy, NOT client requirements:** `main.js` 180 kB · `vendor.js` 250 kB · `main.css` 50 kB (`bundlesize` in `package.json`). (These were set as aspirational targets early in the project. As of the last measurement the actual sizes are well above these ceilings (`main.js` ~352 kB, `vendor.js` ~2 MB) before any optimisation pass — the ceilings need to be re-baselined against measured size + a growth-only headroom (e.g. current + 10–15%) once a baseline pass is done.) Their purpose is regression detection, not a client-facing commitment.
**Third-party script weight:** uncapped — tight LCP is the de-facto constraint. See AGENTS.md > Performance for the deferral rule.

=== tsd-architecture §14.1 Topology (519-575) ===
## 14. CI/CD & Environments

This section probably belong to a DevOps TSD, but will put here temporarily until we have one.

### 14.1 Topology

A six-tier environment topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → UAT → Stage → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).

| #   | Tier            | Owner         | Purpose                                                                      | Third-party availability                                              | Deploy trigger                                                              |
| --- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Local**       | Digital       | Feature build on developer machines                                          | All services mocked (MSW stubs)                                       | `npm start`                                                                 |
| 2   | **Dev**         | Digital       | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop`                                                          |
| 3   | **SIT**         | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence                               | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test                  | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
| 4   | **UAT**         | Shared        | Business acceptance across all 6 regions                                     | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox                 | Business approval gate                                                      |
| 5   | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared        | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows    | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox  | Booked 2-week window                                                        |
| 6   | **Prod**        | Live          | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions                    | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate                                               |

Stage is the **contractual performance-test environment** referenced in §9.3 — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

### 14.2 Branch model

GitFlow with explicit back-merges to keep `develop` aligned with production.

| Branch                    | Branched from          | Merges to                                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `feature/*`               | `develop`              | `develop`                                                                       |
| `fix/*`                   | `develop`              | `develop`                                                                       |
| `release/*`               | `develop`              | `main` **and** `develop`                                                        |
| `fix/release-{version}-*` | the `release/*` branch | the `release/*` branch (forward-merged to `develop` via the release back-merge) |
| `hotfix/*`                | `main`                 | `main` **and** `develop`                                                        |
| `develop`, `main`         | —                      | protected; PR-only                                                              |

Release branches are supervised — code logic fixes go on a `fix/release-{version}-*` sub-branch rather than directly on the release branch. Releases and hotfixes always back-merge to `develop` so production fixes flow forward automatically.

### 14.3 CI workflows

**QA workflow (`qa.yml`)** — runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`. Code-correctness checks with no environment dependency:

- Unit tests (Vitest)
- Storybook interaction tests (`play` functions) and component-level accessibility checks via `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`storybook test --ci`)

**SIT gate (`digital-sit.yml`)** — runs on push/PR to `release/**`; on merge to `develop` it also deploys to the **Dev** environment (tier 2 in §14.1). Environment-dependent checks:

- Playwright `p0` priority specs
- Bundle-size check against the ceilings in §9
- Contract tests against the MuleSoft OpenAPI specification
- Lighthouse CI thresholds (Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90)
- Trend gate against the LHCI history server

### 14.4 Deployment

Deployment is via Salesforce Managed Runtime. Each tier maps to its own MRT target:

- **Dev** — deployed on merge to `develop`, gated on a clean SIT gate (§14.3)
- **SIT** — deployed on the NewStore release cadence, isolated from the Digital release path (failures do not block `release/**`)
- **UAT** — deployed for business acceptance; promotion requires Business sign-off
- **Stage** — deployed on a booked 2-week window for full end-to-end testing with live third parties

## 5. Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture

### 5.1 Storefronts

**8 independent SFCC sites across 6 regions**, each with its own currency, tax model, locale set, delivery options, and payment methods. 11 active locales total. US/EU domestic and international are configured as separate SFCC sites (REG-006).

Rest-of-world traffic routes via `/en-ch/` and `/en-ca/` (DMU-013). AU is configured at the root with no locale prefix and serves as the x-default hreflang target (DMU-016).

### 5.2 Entry routing

- **IP geolocation** selects the site on first visit (REG-013).
- **AU is gated** to Oceania IPs only (REG-009) but remains the x-default hreflang target, so gating runs in the application layer rather than at the network. Non-Oceania human visitors are redirected server-side to their matched storefront before AUD pricing renders; verified search-engine and social-unfurler bots are exempt; UA ambiguity fails open (false positives have no SEO cost; missing a real crawler does).
